**PARIS, France (CNN) —** No matter when you visit, Paris has a certain *je ne sais quoi* that makes it special. But time your trip well, and you could find yourself taking part in one of the city’s signature events—perhaps ice-skating in front of the grand façade of the Hôtel de Ville on a crisp winter day.

### Fashion Weeks

Paris is synonymous with style, and fashionistas will be in seventh heaven during the city’s haute couture fashion weeks, held each January and June/July. Celebrity-spotting, admiring the clothes and scrambling for a seat at Galliano are all par for the course—just make sure your image is up to the occasion.

### Bastille Day

If freedom and fireworks are your thing, what better time to be in Paris than July 14, or Bastille Day? Celebrate the storming of the hated prison—a symbol of repression and aristocratic excess. Watch the military parade proceed down the Champs-Élysées, enjoy the Eiffel Tower fireworks from the Champ de Mars, and raise a glass to *liberté, égalité et fraternité*. No guillotines allowed—and most Métro stations are closed, so be prepared to walk home.

### Paris Plages

It remains true that many Paris residents leave the city in August, closing up shop and heading to the beach. For the past few years, however, Paris Plages has brought that holiday atmosphere into the city. Sand dunes, swimming pools and pétanque may be more readily associated with resorts on France’s southern coast, but all can be found along the riverbank from late July until late August each year.

### The FIAC (International Fair of Contemporary Art)

October’s *Foire Internationale d’Art Contemporain* (FIAC) draws gallery owners and contemporary art collectors to the Louvre and the Grand Palais for one of the art world’s major events. The fair places particular emphasis on up-and-coming artists and newer galleries from across Europe. Works in every medium—including painting, drawing, prints, photography, sculpture and more—are displayed and available for purchase.

### Ice-Skating in Front of the Hôtel de Ville

If you prefer your outdoor pursuits frosty and free, you will love the ice rink outside the Hôtel de Ville, open every year from December until March. Rent a pair of skates or bring your own, then glide around the rink hand in hand with a loved one while admiring the beautiful buildings surrounding the square. Afterwards, warm up with a *chocolat chaud* at a nearby café. Could Paris be any more romantic?

**PARIS, France (CNN) —** Paris has an unmistakable charm in every season, but choosing the right dates can allow visitors to experience one of the capital’s celebrated annual events.

### Fashion Weeks

Paris is synonymous with style, and fashion devotees are especially well served during the city’s haute couture weeks, held each year in January and again in June or July. Expect celebrity sightings, admiration of the latest designs and fierce competition for a place at Galliano’s show. Just be sure your own appearance meets the occasion.

### Bastille Day

For anyone who enjoys freedom-themed celebrations and spectacular fireworks, July 14—Bastille Day—is an ideal time to visit. The holiday commemorates the storming of the despised prison that represented oppression and aristocratic extravagance. Visitors can watch troops parade along the Champs-Élysées, view the Eiffel Tower fireworks from the Champ de Mars and toast *liberté, égalité et fraternité*. Guillotines, of course, are not welcome. Because most Metro stations are closed, plan on walking home.

### Paris Plages

Many Parisians still leave the capital in August, closing their businesses and departing for the seaside. In recent years, however, Paris Plages has brought the atmosphere of a beach vacation into the city itself. From late July through late August, the riverbank offers sand dunes, swimming pools and pétanque—features more commonly associated with resorts on France’s southern coast.

### FIAC: International Fair of Contemporary Art

Every October, the *Foire Internationale d’Art Contemporain*, or FIAC, attracts contemporary-art collectors and gallery owners to the Louvre and the Grand Palais for one of the international art calendar’s leading events. The fair particularly highlights emerging artists and newer galleries from throughout Europe. Paintings, drawings, prints, photographs, sculptures and works in many other media are exhibited and offered for sale.

### Ice-skating at the Hôtel de Ville

Those seeking a chilly outdoor activity that costs nothing can visit the rink installed outside the Hôtel de Ville from December until March. Bring skates or hire a pair, then circle the ice hand in hand with someone special while taking in the elegant architecture surrounding the square. Afterwards, stop at a nearby café for a warming *chocolat chaud*. Few experiences could feel more traditionally Parisian—or more romantic.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style travel article about the best annual events and seasonal attractions in Paris, including Fashion Week, Bastille Day, Paris Plages, FIAC, and ice skating at Hôtel de Ville.
counterfactuals.output:
# Paris by season: The best annual events in the City of Light

Paris doesn’t need a special occasion to draw a crowd. But time a visit around one of the French capital’s signature events and the city can feel transformed — into a global runway, an open-air beach, a contemporary art fair or a giant national celebration.

From summer fireworks over the Eiffel Tower to winter skating beneath ornate façades, here are the annual events and seasonal attractions worth planning a Paris trip around.

## Fashion Week: When Paris becomes the world’s runway

**When:** Several times a year, mainly from January through October

Paris Fashion Week isn’t a single event but a series of men’s, haute couture and women’s ready-to-wear calendars staged throughout the year. The highest-profile women’s shows generally take place in late February or early March and again in late September or early October.

Most runway presentations are invitation-only, but visitors don’t need a front-row seat to enjoy the atmosphere. The spectacle spills into the streets around the Louvre, Place Vendôme, the Grand Palais and the fashionable 1st and 8th arrondissements, where photographers cluster outside venues and cafés become informal meeting rooms for editors, models and buyers.

Travelers can join the mood by visiting exhibitions at the Palais Galliera, shopping designer boutiques along Avenue Montaigne or browsing vintage stores in the Marais.

**Travel tip:** Fashion Week can push up hotel prices, particularly near central show venues. Book early — or stay in a neighborhood such as Canal Saint-Martin or the 11th arrondissement for a less frenetic base.

## Bastille Day: Fireworks, parades and firefighters’ balls

**When:** July 14

France’s national holiday is Paris at its most ceremonial — and most exuberant.

The day traditionally begins with a major military parade along the Avenue des Champs-Élysées, while aircraft fly overhead trailing the blue, white and red of the French flag. In the evening, crowds gather around the Champ de Mars, Trocadéro and the Seine for fireworks centered on the Eiffel Tower, often accompanied by music.

The celebrations frequently begin the night before with **bals des pompiers**, or firefighters’ balls, hosted at fire stations across the city. Some feel like neighborhood parties; others attract long lines and continue into the early hours.

Expect road closures, crowded Metro stations and security checks. A picnic near the Eiffel Tower may sound appealing, but prime viewing areas fill many hours in advance.

**Travel tip:** For a less congested evening, look for elevated viewpoints farther from the center, while respecting any access restrictions announced for the holiday.

## Paris Plages: A summer beach without the sea

**When:** Usually July and August

When temperatures rise, sections of the Seine and other city waterways take on a resort atmosphere during **Paris Plages**.

The annual program typically brings deck chairs, parasols, greenery, games and family activities to waterside locations, often including the Parc Rives de Seine and the Bassin de la Villette. Depending on the year’s program and water conditions, there may also be swimming areas, kayaking or other aquatic activities.

It isn’t a beach in the Mediterranean sense — sand is not guaranteed at every site — but the appeal is distinctly Parisian: reading beside the river, playing pétanque, cooling off at misting stations and watching boats move through the city.

**Travel tip:** Events and locations can change annually. Check the City of Paris program before visiting, particularly for swimming rules, opening hours and heat-related closures.

## FIAC and Paris’ autumn art season

**When:** October

For decades, the **Foire Internationale d’Art Contemporain**, better known as **FIAC**, was one of the marquee events on the Paris cultural calendar, bringing leading galleries and collectors to the city each autumn.

FIAC itself has not been held since 2021. Its October slot was taken over in 2022 by **Paris+ par Art Basel**, now called **Art Basel Paris**, which has continued the tradition of turning the capital into an international contemporary art hub.

The main fair is only part of the experience. Satellite fairs, gallery openings, public installations and museum exhibitions spread across the city, from the Grand Palais area and the Tuileries Garden to the Marais and emerging art districts.

Even without tickets, visitors can spend a rewarding day gallery-hopping along Rue de Turenne and Rue Vieille du Temple, then head to major institutions such as the Bourse de Commerce, Palais de Tokyo or Centre Pompidou — though the latter’s operating status should be checked because of its long-planned renovation.

**Travel tip:** Reserve timed museum entries and fair tickets well ahead. October also brings cooler weather and fewer summer crowds, making it one of the most comfortable times to explore Paris on foot.

## Ice skating at Hôtel de Ville: A beloved winter memory

**When:** Historically during the Christmas and New Year period

For years, one of Paris’ most photogenic winter attractions was the temporary ice rink outside **Hôtel de Ville**, the city’s grand Renaissance Revival town hall. Skaters could glide beneath its elaborate façade in the heart of Paris, within walking distance of Notre Dame and the Marais.

However, the Hôtel de Ville rink has not remained a reliable annual fixture in recent years. Visitors should not assume it will return each winter.

Paris still offers seasonal skating elsewhere, with temporary rinks appearing at locations that may include holiday markets, shopping centers or major venues. Recent winters have featured large-scale skating attractions at sites such as the Grand Palais, depending on construction schedules and annual programming.

Hôtel de Ville itself remains worth visiting during the festive season for lights, decorations and occasional holiday installations.

**Travel tip:** Winter attractions change from year to year. Consult the official Paris tourism and City of Paris websites before packing your skates.

## The best time to go

There is no single perfect season in Paris.

Come in **winter** for couture, festive lights and fewer tourists. Visit in **spring** for café terraces, gardens and ready-to-wear fashion buzz. Choose **summer** for Bastille Day and Paris Plages, accepting hotter weather and larger crowds. Or arrive in **autumn**, when contemporary art takes center stage and the city settles into a more local rhythm.

The key is to plan around what Paris does best: turning the calendar into theater.

counterfactuals.output:
The best times to visit Paris for the richest mix of festivals, cultural events, and seasonal activities are **late May through mid-July** and **September through early October**.

### Best overall: Late May–mid-July
This is Paris’s busiest cultural season, with long days and generally pleasant weather.

Typical highlights include:
- **Roland-Garros/French Open** — late May to early June  
- **Nuit Blanche** — usually the first Saturday in June; all-night contemporary art events  
- **Fête de la Musique** — **June 21**, with free concerts across the city  
- **Paris Pride** — usually late June  
- **Paris Jazz Festival** and other outdoor music programs — summer  
- **Bastille Day** — **July 14**, featuring military ceremonies, concerts, and fireworks near the Eiffel Tower  
- **Paris Plages** — summer pop-up beaches and recreation along the Seine and canals  
- Outdoor cinema, garden events, festivals, and long café evenings  

**Trade-offs:** This period brings high hotel prices, large crowds, and occasional heat waves.

### Best for culture with fewer summer crowds: September–early October
The city returns from the August holiday period, and the cultural calendar becomes very active.

Highlights often include:
- **Journées Européennes du Patrimoine** — usually the third weekend in September; normally closed historic buildings open to visitors  
- **Paris Fashion Week** — late September or early October  
- New exhibitions, theater, opera, ballet, and concert seasons  
- **Fête des Vendanges de Montmartre** — usually October, celebrating the Montmartre grape harvest  
- Pleasant weather and a more local atmosphere than midsummer  

This is arguably the **best balance of events, weather, and city life**.

### Other seasons worth considering

**March–May**
- Spring blossoms and gardens, especially in April  
- Paris Marathon, Easter events, art fairs, and museum programming  
- Mild but changeable weather  
- May includes many public holidays, which can affect opening hours  

**Late July–August**
- Tour de France finish, summer concerts, Paris Plages, outdoor cinema, and **Rock en Seine** in late August  
- Quieter streets in some residential areas  
- Some independent restaurants and shops close for holidays, and hot weather is possible  

**November–December**
- **Paris Photo**, seasonal exhibitions, Christmas lights, department-store windows, markets, ice-skating installations, and holiday concerts  
- Best for a festive winter atmosphere, though days are short and weather is cool and damp  

**January–February**
- Winter sales, Fashion Week, Lunar New Year celebrations, and fewer tourists  
- Usually the least expensive period, but colder and less suited to outdoor activities  

### Simple recommendation
- Choose **June** for the greatest concentration of major public festivals and outdoor events.  
- Choose **late September** for major cultural events with generally better crowd levels.  
- Choose **early December** for holiday lights and seasonal atmosphere.

Exact festival dates can shift each year, so check official event calendars before booking—especially for Fashion Week, Nuit Blanche, Pride, sporting events, and museum festivals.

counterfactuals.output:
# Paris Through the Seasons: Five Signature Events

Paris celebrates nearly everything—sport, music, revolution, wine, and the simple pleasure of filling the streets. These five annual events offer a lively cross-section of the city.

## 1. Schneider Electric Marathon de Paris

**When:** Usually the first or second Sunday in April  
**Where:** Starts on the **Champs-Élysées**, then passes major sights including Place de la Concorde, the Bois de Vincennes, Notre-Dame, the Eiffel Tower, and the Bois de Boulogne.

Even if you are not running, the Paris Marathon is a citywide spectacle. Crowds line the route with signs, music, and plenty of encouragement as tens of thousands of runners pass some of the capital’s most famous landmarks.

**Visitor tips**
- Consult the route map before traveling: road closures and bus diversions are extensive.
- The Métro is usually the easiest way to move between viewing points.
- Good spectator areas include the Bastille, the Seine embankments, and the final stretch near Avenue Foch.
- Arrive early for a clear view and bring snacks; cafés directly along the route can be packed.

---

## 2. Roland-Garros

**When:** Late May to early June; generally a two-week tournament  
**Where:** **Stade Roland-Garros**, 16th arrondissement, beside the Bois de Boulogne

The French Open brings elite tennis—and a distinctly Parisian clay-court atmosphere—to the western edge of the city. Matches range from intimate contests on smaller courts to headline showdowns under the roof of Court Philippe-Chatrier.

**Visitor tips**
- Buy tickets only through the official Roland-Garros ticketing platform or authorized channels.
- Grounds passes can offer better value than show-court tickets, particularly during the opening rounds.
- Use Métro line 9 to **Michel-Ange–Auteuil** or **Michel-Ange–Molitor**; allow extra time for security.
- Bring sun protection and a light rain layer. Late-spring weather can change quickly.
- Nearby accommodation is limited and expensive, so staying elsewhere along line 9 can be more convenient.

---

## 3. Fête de la Musique

**When:** **21 June** every year  
**Where:** Across Paris—especially the Marais, Latin Quarter, Canal Saint-Martin, Montmartre, and major public squares

On the summer solstice, Paris becomes one enormous open-air concert. Professional acts, student bands, choirs, DJs, and enthusiastic amateurs perform in streets, courtyards, bars, churches, and Métro stations. Most performances are free.

**Visitor tips**
- Check the city’s official program shortly before the event, but leave room for spontaneous discoveries.
- Begin early in a residential neighborhood, then move toward larger evening concerts.
- Wear comfortable shoes: crowded streets often make walking faster than buses or taxis.
- Keep valuables secure in dense crowds.
- Métro service is commonly extended, although not every station or line runs all night.
- If you value sleep, avoid booking a room directly above a busy bar or square.

---

## 4. Bastille Day Celebrations

**When:** **14 July**; firefighters’ balls often begin on **13 July**  
**Where:** Military parade on the **Champs-Élysées**; evening fireworks centered on the **Eiffel Tower** and Champ de Mars; bals des pompiers at fire stations citywide

France’s national holiday combines ceremony with celebration. The morning military parade is followed by neighborhood festivities, concerts, firefighters’ balls, and a spectacular nighttime fireworks display around the Eiffel Tower.

**Visitor tips**
- For the parade, arrive very early and expect security checks and station closures.
- The Champ de Mars offers a dramatic fireworks view but becomes extremely crowded. Alternatives include elevated viewpoints and Seine-side locations outside restricted zones.
- Bring water, but check current rules on bottles, glass, and bags before entering controlled areas.
- Reserve dinner well ahead—or eat early—because many restaurants close or fill quickly.
- Walking may be the only practical option after the fireworks, so stay within a manageable distance of your hotel.

---

## 5. Fête des Vendanges de Montmartre

**When:** Usually five days in **early to mid-October**  
**Where:** Around **Sacré-Cœur**, the Clos Montmartre vineyard, and streets throughout the 18th arrondissement

Montmartre’s grape-harvest festival celebrates the tiny Clos Montmartre vineyard with parades, tastings, concerts, exhibitions, food stalls, and neighborhood performances. It feels both festive and local, especially away from the busiest Sacré-Cœur steps.

**Visitor tips**
- Many outdoor activities are free, but tastings and special events may require tickets.
- Explore side streets around Lamarck-Caulaincourt and Jules Joffrin for a less congested experience.
- Montmartre is steep and cobbled; sturdy shoes are essential.
- Use Métro line 12 where possible. The Abbesses station has a long staircase, though a lift is available.
- Visit during a weekday afternoon for smaller crowds; weekends are livelier but much busier.

## Planning Notes

Event dates—apart from fixed celebrations such as **21 June** and **14 July**—can shift each year. Confirm schedules, ticket releases, transport changes, and security restrictions on official event and City of Paris websites before traveling. For major dates, reserve accommodation several months ahead, especially near Roland-Garros, the Champs-Élysées, the Eiffel Tower, and Montmartre.

Paris has a packed annual calendar spanning fashion, national celebrations, art, music, sport, and seasonal festivities:

### Winter
- **Haute Couture Week — January:** The major couture houses present elaborate spring–summer collections, largely at invitation-only runway shows. Fashion exhibitions, street style, and related events animate central Paris.
- **Lunar New Year — January or February:** Parades and festivities are especially lively in the 13th arrondissement, Belleville, and the Marais.
- **Winter ice skating — December to early March:** Temporary rinks appear at changing locations, sometimes including spectacular venues such as the Grand Palais, La Défense, or Christmas markets. Locations and dates vary each year.

### Spring
- **Paris Fashion Week — late February/March:** Autumn–winter womenswear collections draw designers, buyers, celebrities, and photographers from around the world.
- **Paris Marathon — April:** Tens of thousands of runners follow a route past major landmarks, usually beginning near the Champs-Élysées.
- **Foire de Paris — late April/May:** A large public fair devoted to interiors, crafts, food, inventions, and international cultures.
- **Roland-Garros — late May/early June:** The French Open brings the world’s leading tennis players to the clay courts at Porte d’Auteuil.

### Summer
- **Fête de la Musique — June 21:** Free performances fill streets, squares, churches, bars, and concert halls on the summer solstice.
- **Haute Couture Week — late June or July:** Fashion houses unveil their autumn–winter couture collections.
- **Bastille Day — July 14:** France’s national day features a military parade on the Champs-Élysées, public dances and firefighters’ balls, and a major evening fireworks display around the Eiffel Tower and Champ de Mars.
- **Paris Plages — July and August:** Sections of the Seine riverbanks and the Bassin de la Villette become summer leisure areas with deckchairs, games, cultural activities, and sometimes swimming facilities.
- **Tour de France finale — July:** The race traditionally concludes in Paris, though the precise final route can change.
- **Open-air cinema and festivals — July/August:** Parc de la Villette and other venues host outdoor films, concerts, and cultural programs.

### Autumn
- **European Heritage Days — September:** Historic government buildings, private mansions, workshops, and other normally restricted sites open to visitors.
- **Paris Fashion Week — September/October:** Spring–summer womenswear shows make this one of the city’s most visible fashion periods.
- **Nuit Blanche — usually in early autumn:** A night of free contemporary art installations and performances in public spaces; timing and format can vary.
- **Art Basel Paris — October:** A leading modern and contemporary art fair, held at the Grand Palais, with galleries, installations, and satellite events across the city.
- **Montmartre Grape Harvest Festival — October:** The *Fête des Vendanges* celebrates Montmartre’s small vineyard with parades, tastings, music, and fireworks.
- **Paris Photo — November:** One of the world’s foremost photography fairs, bringing galleries, publishers, collectors, and artists to Paris.

### Holiday season
- **Christmas markets and illuminations — late November/December:** Festive displays appear along major avenues and around department stores such as Galeries Lafayette and Printemps.
- **New Year’s Eve — December 31:** Crowds gather around the Champs-Élysées and Arc de Triomphe for projections, celebrations, and—depending on the year—fireworks.

Exact dates, venues, and public-access arrangements change annually, especially for fashion shows, art fairs, ice rinks, and outdoor celebrations.

# Paris Events Calendar

Paris is never out of season. January brings fashion, winter sales, and glowing streets; summer fills the riverbanks with music and outdoor festivals; October celebrates art, wine, and the return of cultural life; and winter transforms the capital into a festive city of lights. Here’s what travelers can see and do throughout the year.

## January: Sales, Style, and Quiet Museums

January is one of the calmest times to explore Paris. With fewer visitors, travelers can linger in the Louvre, Musée d’Orsay, and Centre Pompidou without the peak-season crowds. Crisp walks along the Seine are especially rewarding when the city is wrapped in winter light.

The month is also known for the **winter sales**, or *soldes d’hiver*, when department stores and boutiques offer major discounts. Head to Galeries Lafayette, Printemps, Le Marais, or Saint-Germain-des-Prés for fashion bargains.

Other January highlights include:

- **Paris Fashion Week**, which brings designers, models, and photographers to the city  
- **Epiphany celebrations**, featuring *galette des rois*, a puff-pastry cake traditionally shared in cafés and homes  
- **Seasonal concerts and opera**, from intimate church performances to productions at the Palais Garnier  
- **Ice-skating rinks and festive displays**, some of which continue after New Year  

Pack a warm coat and waterproof shoes, then enjoy the rare pleasure of seeing Paris at a slower pace.

## Summer: Festivals, Riverbanks, and Long Evenings

Summer turns Paris into an open-air playground. Long daylight hours make it easy to combine sightseeing with picnics, concerts, and late dinners on café terraces.

A centerpiece of the season is **Paris Plages**, when sections of the Seine and Canal de l’Ourcq are transformed with deck chairs, greenery, activities, and waterside entertainment. It is not quite the Riviera, but it offers a playful urban version of a beach holiday.

Travelers can also look forward to:

- **Fête de la Musique** in June, with free performances in streets, squares, bars, and courtyards  
- **Bastille Day** on July 14, marked by a military parade, public dances, and fireworks near the Eiffel Tower  
- **Outdoor cinema**, including screenings in Parc de la Villette  
- **Summer music festivals**, featuring jazz, classical music, rock, and electronic acts  
- **The final stage of the Tour de France**, traditionally ending on the Champs-Élysées  
- **Nighttime fountain shows and garden events** at destinations such as Versailles  

Summer is popular, so reserve major attractions and restaurants in advance. During hot afternoons, visit shaded parks or air-conditioned museums, then return outdoors as the evening cools.

## October: Art, Harvest Flavors, and Cultural Energy

October feels like a second beginning in Paris. The summer crowds thin, theaters launch new programs, galleries unveil exhibitions, and autumn colors spread through the Luxembourg Gardens and Parc des Buttes-Chaumont.

One of the month’s most distinctive events is **Nuit Blanche**, an all-night celebration of contemporary art. Installations and performances appear in museums, public buildings, and unexpected spaces across the city. The event’s timing can vary, so check the annual schedule.

October may also feature:

- **Montmartre’s Fête des Vendanges**, celebrating the neighborhood’s tiny vineyard with parades, tastings, concerts, and street entertainment  
- **Major contemporary-art fairs and gallery events**  
- **Autumn exhibitions** at leading museums  
- **Salon du Chocolat**, a popular showcase for chocolatiers and pastry chefs, often held in late October or early November  
- **Halloween activities** at theme parks, family attractions, and selected venues  

This is an excellent month for food-focused travel. Warm up with onion soup, roasted chestnuts, hot chocolate, and seasonal pastries after a day of gallery-hopping.

## Winter: Christmas Markets and a City of Lights

From late November through December—and often into early January—Paris embraces the festive season. Grand avenues sparkle with illuminations, shop windows become miniature theaters, and Christmas markets serve mulled wine, cheese, sweets, and handcrafted gifts.

Don’t miss:

- **Holiday lights on the Champs-Élysées and around central Paris**  
- **Animated department-store windows** at Galeries Lafayette and Printemps  
- **Christmas markets**, which vary by year and location  
- **Nativity scenes and seasonal concerts** in historic churches  
- **New Year’s Eve celebrations**, particularly around major landmarks and nightlife districts  
- **Winter cruises on the Seine**, offering illuminated views from a heated boat  

Winter is also ideal for classic indoor pleasures: browsing covered passages, sipping hot chocolate in an old café, attending the ballet, or exploring smaller museums.

Event dates and locations can change each year, so travelers should consult official tourism and venue websites before booking. Whatever the season, Paris provides a calendar filled with art, food, music, fashion, and unforgettable street life.
